justice: The street allocates substantial space to motor traffic with multiple wide vehicle lanes, while the pedestrian realm on the right appears comparatively narrow, indicating an uneven distribution of street space among road users.
A separated side path and sidewalk are visible on the right side, which gives non-motorized users some dedicated space instead of forcing them into the carriageway.

Accessibility is only moderate because the visible sidewalk looks smooth and level, but no curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or other barrier-free crossing features can be seen in this view.
safety: Lane markings are clear and the roadway is wide and orderly, which helps drivers maintain predictable movement and reduces immediate conflict risk.
Streetlights are installed continuously along the corridor, supporting visibility and perceived safety after dark.

Safety is weakened by the high-speed arterial character: multiple broad lanes and long uninterrupted sightlines encourage faster vehicle movement, while no visible pedestrian crossing or refuge island is present in the scene.
livability: The corridor feels dominated by through-traffic movement rather than everyday street life, with very wide asphalt carriageways and little visible frontage activity.
Trees and planted medians on both sides add greenery and soften the road environment, which supports basic environmental quality.
Livability is limited because no benches, bus stops, storefronts, public gathering spaces, or visible social activity are present in the image.
sustainability: Continuous rows of trees and planted shrubs along the median and roadside provide green infrastructure and some ecological value.
A separate side path on the right can support active travel, which is more sustainable than a fully car-only corridor.
Sustainability is constrained by the large amount of paved space devoted to motor vehicles and the absence of clearly visible public transport facilities such as bus lanes or bus stops.
aesthetics: The boulevard has a clean, orderly appearance with consistent lane markings, coordinated streetlights, and maintained planting beds.
Tree rows on both sides frame the street and improve visual quality compared with a fully barren roadway.
Aesthetics are reduced somewhat by the dominance of expansive asphalt and the relatively monotonous linear road scene with limited architectural or human-scale detail.
comfort: Thermal comfort is mixed: mature trees on the right and in the median provide some shade, but the broad exposed roadway and sidewalk areas remain heavily sunlit.
Physical comfort is supported by the smooth asphalt roadway and the paved side path, which appear even and unobstructed for movement.
Psychological comfort is only moderate because the street is very wide and traffic-oriented, with long open lanes and moving motor vehicles creating a less intimate environment for non-drivers.
walkability: A continuous sidewalk or side path is visible on the right, so pedestrians appear to have a dedicated route separated from the main carriageway.
Walkability is weakened by the arterial scale of the street: the crossing distance would be long, and no zebra crossing, pedestrian signal, or median refuge is visible in this frame.
The walking environment lacks pedestrian-oriented amenities such as benches, active building edges, or clearly marked access points, making it functional but not especially inviting for walking.
